findings.finding: The decision relies on an unverified claim about what revocation does: that 'revoking would invalidate a legitimate identity'. The shipped era model contradicts it. Revocation is position-scoped, so revoking at the rotated key's add position (1788820816306746425-…) would only reject certs stored at or after that position. Pre-rotation certs and identity would stay valid. The plan does not reconcile this claim with the code or the ADR.
findings.location: Decision (recorded 2026-11-19 PST) — 'revoking would invalidate a legitimate identity'
scenarios: A reader of the decision record wrongly concludes that position-scoped revocation is destructive. Rotated-out keys then stay trusted by default in future rotations as well.
The old private key, still in SSM or a backup, signs a new op-cert or authorship event after 2026-09-07. It verifies as certified because no revoke boundary exists.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the Decision section: (1) the position of the last op-cert signed by 61689bf468f5, found by scanning the op-cert SIGNATURE events; (2) a statement that, under the opcert.py rule, revoking at the rotated key's add position leaves every cert stored before that position valid; (3) the operator's reason for keeping the key unrevoked given (1) and (2), or a revised decision.

Retrieved: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 (https://mtg.de/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/NIST.SP_.800-57pt1r5.pdf). The search summary at https://cubixbot.com/nist-sp-800-57-key-management-guidelines/ describes the 'Originator-Usage Period (OUP): the specific time window during which a key can be actively used to … generat[e] new digital signatures'.
Plan Context: 'it is still trusted for every position after that date' and 'An unrevoked rotated key widens that trust as well' (authorship trust from starving-sphalerite-skua).
findings.finding: The plan does not weigh established practice for rotating signing keys. In that practice, a rotated-out key stops being trusted for NEW signatures at rotation while its old signatures stay verifiable. NIST SP 800-57 calls this the originator-usage period vs. the recipient-usage period, and the repo's ADR 0049 describes the same idea as 'routine rotation, history intact'. The decision treats the choice as 'revoke and break history' vs. 'keep trusted forever' and never considers the standard middle option that the existing era fields already support.
scenarios: Every future rotation copies this precedent, and trusted_environments.yaml collects old keys that can never expire.
Authorship signing by environment keys (starving-sphalerite-skua) inherits the unbounded era of every rotated-out key.
